Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are
$\displaystyle
 \lim_{x\to 0}  \ln\left(x^2\right) = -\infty$ and $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2}{x^2} = \infty$ respectively,
so we have the case $\dfrac{-\infty}{\infty}$.

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} &= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{[\ln\left(x^2\right)]'}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{\left(1/x^2\right)\cdot 2x}{-\left({4}/{x^3}\right)}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{x^{-2} \cdot 2x}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{2x^{-1}}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt]
&= -\dfrac{1}{2}  \lim_{x\to 0} {x^2}\[5pt]
&= -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0\[5pt]
&= 0.
}
$$
